title: Spending Money on Others
text:
In 2008 Elizabeth Dunn, Lara Aknin and Michael Norton published a short paper in Science asking whether how people spend money affects how happy they are. They started with a national survey of more than six hundred Americans. How much people spent on themselves did not predict their happiness, but how much they spent on gifts for others and on charity did.

They then followed employees at a company in Boston who received a profit-sharing bonus. Those who spent more of it on others reported being happier weeks later, regardless of the bonus size.

Finally, they ran an experiment at the University of British Columbia in Vancouver. In the morning, students were handed an envelope with either 5 or 20 dollars. Some were told to spend it on a bill, an expense or a gift for themselves by five o'clock. Others were told to spend it on a gift for someone else or a donation. That evening, those who had spent the money on others reported being happier than those who had spent it on themselves. The amount did not matter. Yet when other students were asked to predict the results, most expected spending on oneself, and more money, to bring more happiness.
lesson: Spending a little on someone else tends to lift your mood more than spending it on yourself. Even a small gift or treat for another person counts.
people: Elizabeth Dunn, Lara Aknin, Michael Norton
location: University of British Columbia, Vancouver, Canada, and Boston, USA
source: Dunn, E. W., Aknin, L. B., and Norton, M. I. (2008). Spending money on others promotes happiness. Science, 319(5870), 1687-1688.
caveat: The experiment was small; later studies in many countries support the link, though its size varies.
place: University of British Columbia, Vancouver, Canada
